messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Community Organizer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Darkness: Dark spaces, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people, Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nabil is a 54-year-old Arab American man who has spent years working as a community organizer, someone used to being recognized in neighborhood meetings, churches, school gyms, and city offices as steady, persuasive, and available to others. He is married now and speaks about his current home life carefully, as if testing whether safety can really last. The event he returns to in treatment came from an earlier romantic relationship marked by physical abuse. He describes one night in particular at the apartment where they had been living, a place he no longer passes if he can help it. It was dark inside, with most of the lights off, and he remembers the feeling of being trapped in rooms that had suddenly become unfamiliar. What remains most sharply with him is not a single clear sequence but bits of the night: the sense of being cornered in that apartment, the shock that the person hurting him was someone he had trusted, and the sounds that accompanied it. In his memory he hears the same noises again, especially the thudding chaos in the room and, outside, the chop of a helicopter overhead or an aircraft passing low enough that it fused with the terror of that moment. He says the pieces do not line up into one complete story. Instead they come as scattered fragments, vivid and disconnected.

In the weeks afterward, Nabil found that certain things could pull the whole scene back without warning. Darkness was especially difficult. Walking into an unlit hallway, entering a dim parking area after an evening meeting, or waking in the night before his eyes adjusted could bring an immediate jolt, as if the apartment were around him again. Specific places also carried a force he could not explain away. The block where the abuse happened, nearby streets, and buildings with a similar layout made his body tense before he had fully registered where he was. Aircraft sounds were another problem. During outdoor events for work, when a helicopter crossed overhead, he would abruptly lose his sense of the present and hear in his head the sounds from that night, layered over what was actually happening around him.

He had come to believe that what happened said something fundamental and damning about him. He spoke bitterly about having been betrayed by someone he loved, but beneath that was a harsher conclusion: that this was the kind of thing that happened because of the sort of person he was. He did not describe this as a passing thought. It had settled into the way he understood himself. He also said that his assumptions about people had been destroyed. Before, he had believed closeness offered protection, that home was where danger ended; afterward, he felt that the world no longer followed rules he could trust.

Over months, his daily life narrowed around efforts to feel less exposed. He became vigilant around other people, scanning faces, posture, tone, and proximity for any sign that someone might turn dangerous. At work this showed up constantly. Community organizing requires entering unfamiliar buildings, knocking on doors, standing in crowds, and staying late after meetings when schools and recreation centers empty out and the hallways dim. Nabil began arriving with extra layers on, choosing concealing clothing that made him feel less noticeable and less readable to others. He positioned himself near exits and tracked who came into a room. Colleagues noticed that he sometimes cut conversations short or left suddenly after hearing aircraft overhead. He also rerouted his travel across the city to avoid the site of the abuse entirely, adding time to his commute and sometimes declining meetings on that side of town. He told himself there was no reason to go near that block and no reason to test what would happen.

At home, his wife saw how quickly his attention shifted when the house was dark or when sounds from outside changed. He was not describing a single clean memory to her, because he did not have one. He had shards: the dark, the apartment, the betrayal, the sounds in his head. What frightened him most was how instantly the past could arrive, with no warning from his own mind before something in the environment pulled it in.

He sought help after a recent evening event for tenants’ rights held in a church basement. When the meeting ended and people filtered out, the room dimmed, and a helicopter passed overhead. For a moment he was no longer in the basement but back inside that apartment, hearing the old sounds in his head and feeling sure he was in danger. He recovered enough to leave, but afterward he was shaken by how completely his surroundings had disappeared. Coming to treatment, he says he wants to understand why these moments still overtake him and whether it is possible to move through his city, do his work, and be with people he loves without feeling that trust is a mistake waiting to be punished.
